Prompt: Realm9 Website Content Redesign

Redesign and implement the website content only in realm9-nextjs. Do NOT modify colate/realm9 or redesign the UI yet. Our priority is to finalize meaningful, professional marketing content across all pages before working on the visual design.

Use colate/realm9 as the source of truth for Realm9's actual capabilities, features, modules, statistics, and product positioning. Review the existing application and identify newly introduced capabilities that are missing from the current marketing website.

Content requirements:

Modules section: Rewrite and enhance the module names, descriptions, and supporting content shown in the screenshot. Clearly communicate what each module does and the value it provides to customers.
Existing pages: Review and improve the hero headings, descriptions, section content, and CTAs. Preserve the meaning of Realm9's existing content while making it more compelling, concise, and premium.
New capabilities: Incorporate relevant features introduced in colate/realm9 that are not yet represented on the marketing website.
New pages: Develop meaningful, audience-specific marketing content for pages such as Startups and other routes that were not part of the original Realm9 website. Ensure every page accurately communicates how Realm9 serves its intended audience.
Statistics: Use only verified statistics and product claims from colate/realm9. Do not invent metrics, capabilities, or customer claims.

Content direction: Take inspiration from the existing Realm9 website, but do not simply copy its wording. Rewrite the content to reflect Realm9's current capabilities and give the website a fresh, premium, enterprise-grade identity that meets professional SaaS marketing standards.

Every page should help a potential customer immediately understand what Realm9 offers, what problems it solves, how its capabilities benefit them, and why they should explore the platform further.

First, audit the existing website content against colate/realm9, identify missing or outdated information, and then implement the improved content across all relevant pages in realm9-nextjs.

Important: Focus exclusively on content, messaging, and page structure. Preserve the existing UI, styling, routes, and functionality. We will work on the visual redesign separately after the content is finalized
continue
I'll start by exploring both projects to understand the current state of realm9-nextjs and colate/realm9, then audit the content and build a comprehensive plan.

  3	## ⚠️ CRITICAL DEVELOPMENT PRINCIPLES
  4	
  5	### DISTRIBUTED SYSTEMS & PRODUCTION THINKING
  6	**CRITICAL**: Always design for production multi-pod/multi-instance deployments:
  7	
  8	**Before implementing ANY stateful operation, ask yourself:**
  9	1. ✅ **What if multiple pods/instances run this simultaneously?**
 10	   - Will it cause race conditions?
 11	   - Will one pod interfere with another's work?
 12	   - Is there shared state that needs coordination?
 13	
 14	2. ✅ **What if a pod restarts mid-operation?**
 15	   - Will orphaned data be left behind?
 16	   - How will cleanup work without affecting other pods?
 17	   - Is there a recovery mechanism?
 18	
 19	3. ✅ **What if operations span multiple requests/pods?**
 20	   - Is there proper state tracking (database, not in-memory)?
 21	   - Can operations be resumed after pod failure?
 22	   - Are there proper locks/coordination mechanisms?
 23	
 24	**Common Anti-Patterns to AVOID:**
 25	- ❌ **In-memory state only**: Use database/Redis for shared state
 26	- ❌ **Cleanup on startup without checks**: One pod shouldn't kill another pod's work
 27	- ❌ **Assuming single instance**: Always design for horizontal scaling
 28	- ❌ **File-based locks**: Use database locks or distributed locks (Redis)
 29	- ❌ **Process-level coordination**: Use database/Redis for coordination
 30	- ❌ **Marking all jobs as failed on startup**: Use heartbeat/timeout mechanisms instead
 31	
 32	**Production-Safe Patterns:**
 33	- ✅ **Heartbeat tracking**: Jobs send periodic heartbeats, cleanup only if heartbeat stale
 34	- ✅ **Database-persisted state**: All state in DB/Redis, not in-memory
 35	- ✅ **Distributed locks**: Use database advisory locks or Redis locks
 36	- ✅ **Idempotent operations**: Operations safe to retry/repeat
 37	- ✅ **Graceful degradation**: System works even if some pods fail
 38	- ✅ **Job ownership**: Clear ownership of background jobs (pod ID, timestamps)
 39	
 40	**Examples of Multi-Pod Considerations:**
 41	- **Background Jobs**: Use heartbeat to detect dead jobs (not "mark all as failed on startup")
 42	- **Scheduled Tasks**: Use distributed locks to prevent duplicate execution
 43	- **Caching**: Use Redis, not in-memory cache (or accept stale data across pods)
 44	- **File Uploads**: Use S3/object storage, not local filesystem
 45	- **Session Management**: Use database sessions or Redis, not in-memory
 46	- **Rate Limiting**: Use Redis counters, not in-memory counters
 47	
 48	**When to Use What:**
 49	- **Database**: Persistent state, job tracking, locks, queues
 50	- **Redis**: Fast caching, distributed locks, real-time counters, pub/sub
 51	- **In-Memory**: Read-only data, configuration, temporary computation results
 52	- **File System**: Never for shared state (only for pod-local temporary files)
 53	
 54	**REMEMBER**: Kubernetes/production environments have:
 55	- Multiple pods running simultaneously
 56	- Pods can restart/crash at any time
 57	- Rolling updates (old + new pods running together)
 58	- Auto-scaling (pods added/removed dynamically)
 59	
 60	**Always test your mental model**: "If I have 3 pods and one restarts, does this still work correctly?"
 61	
 62	### BUILD STRATEGY
 63	**IMPORTANT**: Optimize build workflow to save time:
 64	- ✅ **DO**: Only run builds when making significant changes or when explicitly requested
 65	- ✅ **DO**: Focus ONLY on errors during build, ignore warnings unless they're blocking
 66	- ✅ **DO**: Skip builds for small, incremental changes (single line edits, minor fixes)
 67	- ❌ **DO NOT**: Run `npm run build` after every small change
 68	- ❌ **DO NOT**: Report warnings as issues unless they cause actual failures
 69	- ❌ **DO NOT**: Clear `.next` cache unless there's a specific caching issue
 70	
 71	**Build Triggers** (when you SHOULD build):
 72	- Major refactoring or architectural changes
 73	- Adding new dependencies or packages
 74	- Schema changes or database migrations
 75	- User explicitly requests: "build this" or "test the build"
 76	- Before creating a PR or final testing
 77	
 78	**Skip Builds For** (save time):
 79	- Fixing typos or formatting
 80	- Single line code changes
 81	- Adding/updating comments
 82	- Documentation updates
 83	- Small bug fixes in isolated functions
 84	
 85	### DO NOT REMOVE CODE OR FEATURES
 86	**IMPORTANT**: When encountering errors or missing functionality:
 87	- ✅ **DO**: Fix the underlying issue properly
 88	- ✅ **DO**: Add missing relations, fields, or functionality
 89	- ✅ **DO**: Update code to work with existing schema
 90	- ❌ **DO NOT**: Remove features to make errors go away
 91	- ❌ **DO NOT**: Delete schema fields that cause errors
 92	- ❌ **DO NOT**: Comment out functionality instead of fixing it
 93	
 94	**Example**: If `_count.runs` doesn't exist, calculate it from related data rather than removing the runs count feature.
 95	
 96	### DO NOT RESTRUCTURE MID-IMPLEMENTATION
 97	**Discovering that files are growing, or that concerns are muddled, does not authorise changing the execution plan.**
 98	
 99	- ✅ **DO**: make a small, local extraction when it is genuinely trivial and self-contained
100	- ✅ **DO**: finish the work the normal way, then **suggest** the split at the end
101	- ✅ **DO**: fix a split that was planned but planned slightly wrong, when the correction is small
102	- ✅ **DO**: stop and ask when a planned split turns out to need substantially more restructuring than the plan assumed — scale the decision to how large and important it is
103	- ❌ **DO NOT**: begin splitting files, extracting modules, or reorganising responsibilities that the plan did not call for
104	- ❌ **DO NOT**: treat "this file is getting big" as a reason to abandon the agreed sequence
105	
106	**Why**: an unplanned refactor mid-implementation is its own risk — it enlarges the blast radius, mixes structural change into a feature diff so neither can be reviewed cleanly, and makes the plan stop describing the work. Structural change is either **planned up front** or **proposed at the end**. It is never decided halfway through.

47	# Editing this README
48	
49	When you're ready to make this README your own, just edit this file and use the handy template below (or feel free to structure it however you want - this is just a starting point!). Thanks to [makeareadme.com](https://www.makeareadme.com/) for this template.
50	
51	## Suggestions for a good README
52	
53	Every project is different, so consider which of these sections apply to yours. The sections used in the template are suggestions for most open source projects. Also keep in mind that while a README can be too long and detailed, too long is better than too short. If you think your README is too long, consider utilizing another form of documentation rather than cutting out information.
54	
55	## Name
56	Choose a self-explaining name for your project.
57	
58	## Description
59	Let people know what your project can do specifically. Provide context and add a link to any reference visitors might be unfamiliar with. A list of Features or a Background subsection can also be added here. If there are alternatives to your project, this is a good place to list differentiating factors.
60	
61	## Badges
62	On some READMEs, you may see small images that convey metadata, such as whether or not all the tests are passing for the project. You can use Shields to add some to your README. Many services also have instructions for adding a badge.
63	
64	## Visuals
65	Depending on what you are making, it can be a good idea to include screenshots or even a video (you'll frequently see GIFs rather than actual videos). Tools like ttygif can help, but check out Asciinema for a more sophisticated method.
66	
67	## Installation
68	Within a particular ecosystem, there may be a common way of installing things, such as using Yarn, NuGet, or Homebrew. However, consider the possibility that whoever is reading your README is a novice and would like more guidance. Listing specific steps helps remove ambiguity and gets people to using your project as quickly as possible. If it only runs in a specific context like a particular programming language version or operating system or has dependencies that have to be installed manually, also add a Requirements subsection.
69	
70	## Usage
71	Use examples liberally, and show the expected output if you can. It's helpful to have inline the smallest example of usage that you can demonstrate, while providing links to more sophisticated examples if they are too long to reasonably include in the README.
72	
73	## Support
74	Tell people where they can go to for help. It can be any combination of an issue tracker, a chat room, an email address, etc.
75	
76	## Roadmap
77	If you have ideas for releases in the future, it is a good idea to list them in the README.
78	
79	## Contributing
80	State if you are open to contributions and what your requirements are for accepting them.
81	
82	For people who want to make changes to your project, it's helpful to have some documentation on how to get started. Perhaps there is a script that they should run or some environment variables that they need to set. Make these steps explicit. These instructions could also be useful to your future self.
83	
84	You can also document commands to lint the code or run tests. These steps help to ensure high code quality and reduce the likelihood that the changes inadvertently break something. Having instructions for running tests is especially helpful if it requires external setup, such as starting a Selenium server for testing in a browser.
85	
86	## Authors and acknowledgment
87	Show your appreciation to those who have contributed to the project.
88	
89	## License
90	For open source projects, say how it is licensed.
91	
92	## Project status
93	If you have run out of energy or time for your project, put a note at the top of the README saying that development has slowed down or stopped completely. Someone may choose to fork your project or volunteer to step in as a maintainer or owner, allowing your project to keep going. You can also make an explicit request for maintainers.

# Editing this README

When you're ready to make this README your own, just edit this file and use the handy template below (or feel free to structure it however you want - this is ju
st a starting point!). Thanks to [makeareadme.com](https://www.makeareadme.com/) for this template.

## Suggestions for a good README

Every project is different, so consider which of these sections apply to yours. The sections used in the template are suggestions for most open source projects.
 Also keep in mind that while a README can be too long and detailed, too long is better than too short. If you think your README is too long, consider utilizing
 another form of documentation rather than cutting out information.

## Name
Choose a self-explaining name for your project.

## Description
Let people know what your project can do specifically. Provide context and add a link to any reference visitors might be unfamiliar with. A list of Features or
a Background subsection can also be added here. If there are alternatives to your project, this is a good place to list differentiating factors.

## Badges
On some READMEs, you may see small images that convey metadata, such as whether or not all the tests are passing for the project. You can use Shields to add som
e to your README. Many services also have instructions for adding a badge.

## Visuals
Depending on what you are making, it can be a good idea to include screenshots or even a video (you'll frequently see GIFs rather than actual videos). Tools lik
e ttygif can help, but check out Asciinema for a more sophisticated method.

## Installation
Within a particular ecosystem, there may be a common way of installing things, such as using Yarn, NuGet, or Homebrew. However, consider the possibility that wh
oever is reading your README is a novice and would like more guidance. Listing specific steps helps remove ambiguity and gets people to using your project as qu
ickly as possible. If it only runs in a specific context like a particular programming language version or operating system or has dependencies that have to be
installed manually, also add a Requirements subsection.

## Usage
Use examples liberally, and show the expected output if you can. It's helpful to have inline the smallest example of usage that you can demonstrate, while provi
ding links to more sophisticated examples if they are too long to reasonably include in the README.

## Support
Tell people where they can go to for help. It can be any combination of an issue tracker, a chat room, an email address, etc.

## Roadmap
If you have ideas for releases in the future, it is a good idea to list them in the README.

## Contributing
State if you are open to contributions and what your requirements are for accepting them.

For people who want to make changes to your project, it's helpful to have some documentation on how to get started. Perhaps there is a script that they should r
un or some environment variables that they need to set. Make these steps explicit. These instructions could also be useful to your future self.

You can also document commands to lint the code or run tests. These steps help to ensure high code quality and reduce the likelihood that the changes inadverten
tly break something. Having instructions for running tests is especially helpful if it requires external setup, such as starting a Selenium server for testing i
n a browser.

## Authors and acknowledgment
Show your appreciation to those who have contributed to the project.

## License
For open source projects, say how it is licensed.

## Project status
If you have run out of energy or time for your project, put a note at the top of the README saying that development has slowed down or stopped completely. Someo
ne may choose to fork your project or volunteer to step in as a maintainer or owner, allowing your project to keep going. You can also make an explicit request
for maintainers.
